title: Egypt's Sisi Seeks Parliament's Backing to Defend Saudi Arabia if Asked
excerpt: Sisi told a military graduation Egypt would take any measures necessary to defend the kingdom against Houthi attacks, and parliament set an emergency session for Sunday.
body:
• Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday Egypt would take any measures necessary to defend Saudi Arabia if asked, amid escalating Houthi attacks on the kingdom.
  • Sisi asked parliament for authorisation in advance; parliament announced an emergency plenary session for 1 pm on Sunday.
  • The Houthis have attacked Riyadh's international airport and Saudi Aramco in recent days after a truce collapsed and fighting in Yemen reignited.
  • Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen in 2015, and Gulf states have provided Egypt billions in aid, deposits and investment since 2013.

Egypt would take any measures necessary to defend Saudi Arabia if asked, President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday, and he asked parliament to authorise that step in advance as Houthi attacks on the kingdom escalate, Reuters reported.

"It is inconceivable that we would allow Saudi Arabia, its security or stability to be harmed."

— Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, President of Egypt

Sisi spoke at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy. He said Egypt was not seeking to attack anyone, but was prepared to act in defence, and that any action would follow guidance from Saudi King Salman and Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Al Jazeera carried the announcement the same day.

The Parliamentary Step

"I know this requires the approval of the Egyptian parliament, and I ask that an emergency session be held so that it can give us that authorisation if we are asked," Sisi said. Shortly after he spoke, parliament announced a plenary session at 1 pm (1000 GMT) on Sunday in response, though it did not disclose the agenda.

The sequence matters. Sisi is seeking the mandate before any Saudi request arrives, which would let Egypt move immediately if Riyadh asks, rather than opening a parliamentary debate in the middle of a crisis.

The Attacks Behind It

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have attacked Riyadh's international airport and state oil giant Saudi Aramco in recent days, amid renewed fighting with the Saudi-backed forces of Yemen's internationally recognised government following the collapse of a truce. Mohammed bin Salman visited Sisi on September 15, after fighting reignited, to discuss security and Red Sea navigation.

An Old Alliance, Restated

Egypt and Saudi Arabia are close strategic and economic partners. Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states provided Egypt with billions of dollars in aid, central-bank deposits and investments after the military ouster of Islamist president Mohamed Morsi in 2013. Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition that intervened in Yemen in 2015 to support the government against the Houthis.

Red Sea Stakes

The September 15 meeting between Mohammed bin Salman and Sisi covered Red Sea navigation as well as security, Reuters noted. Egypt controls the Suez Canal at the Red Sea's northern end, and Houthi attacks on shipping have already cut the canal's traffic and revenue. A wider Houthi campaign against Saudi targets therefore lands on Egypt's economy as well as its alliance politics, which is part of why Cairo is moving to formalise its position now rather than after a request arrives.

What's Next

Sunday's parliamentary session is the immediate test. An authorisation would widen the circle of states formally committed to Saudi Arabia's defence at a moment when attacks on the kingdom are already disrupting Gulf aviation and energy infrastructure.
